actions.result: Patient reports skipping breakfast most days, small lunch, large dinner (often 8-9 PM) that triggers fullness/discomfort and occasional palpitations; low fruit intake; avoids dairy; limited fluid intake aside from water/tea.

actions.name: Nutrition-focused physical exam (patient self-exam via camera)
actions.result: Patient shows mild temporal wasting and visibly thin forearms on camera; right ankle shows 1+ pitting edema when patient presses on it himself; no visible muscle wasting assessment of calves possible due to swelling.

actions.name: Malnutrition screening (e.g., MST or similar)
actions.result: Score indicates moderate risk: unintentional weight loss >5% in 6 months plus reduced intake pattern (early satiety limiting meal volume).

actions.result: Patient scores in precontemplation to early contemplation stage; acknowledges diet 'matters' but unsure of specific action steps; open to simple, concrete suggestions.

actions.name: Review prior GI workup notes
actions.result: Multiple upper endoscopies over past 2 years, all with normal findings; no structural cause identified for early satiety.

actions.name: Estimate energy and protein needs
actions.result: Estimated needs approximately 1850-2000 kcal/day and 70-80 g protein/day (about 1.1-1.2 g/kg) based on 65.8 kg body weight, adjusted for underweight status and need to preserve lean mass without excess sodium/fluid load.

actions.name: Review home blood glucose log
actions.result: No home glucose monitoring log on file; patient has not been given or is not using a glucometer.

objectives.text: Apply the Nutrition Care Process to synthesize assessment data (weight trend, BMI, labs, intake pattern) into an accurate PES statement reflecting unintended weight loss and inadequate oral intake related to early satiety and poorly controlled diabetes.
Identify the discrepancy between reported medication adherence and refill history for metformin, and explore barriers using motivational interviewing rather than confrontation.
Integrate nutrition care with medication regimen by recognizing how meal timing, metformin timing, and GI symptoms interact without providing medical advice outside scope.

Use motivational interviewing techniques to explore the patient's beliefs that heart disease and diabetes are unrelated, and his fear that weight gain/eating more could worsen his heart failure or cause frailty concerns to be reconciled with unintentional weight loss.

Assess psychosocial and financial barriers (cost of fresh produce, work schedule, fatigue, low health literacy) and tailor recommendations to his stated preference for simple, concrete, non-overwhelming steps.
Identify and appropriately engage available support resources (adult son, community programs) while respecting the patient's value of independence.

scenario.studentBrief: You are a dietetics student conducting a telehealth nutrition assessment for Marcus Ramirez, a 59-year-old man with heart failure and newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes, referred for medical nutrition therapy. He reports early satiety, fatigue, and uncertainty about how diet relates to his conditions. Conduct a full nutrition assessment, identify a nutrition diagnosis using PES format, and provide patient-centered counseling using motivational interviewing.
scenario.chiefComplaint: Early satiety, fatigue, and uncertainty about diet's role in managing newly diagnosed diabetes alongside heart failure
scenario.openingLine: Hi. They said I should talk to a dietitian. I get full real fast when I eat, and I'm tired a lot. Not sure food's really the issue though - that's what the pills are for, right?
tasks: Obtain a thorough diet history including meal pattern, food preferences, fluid intake, and barriers
Review relevant anthropometric data, labs, and medication list with the patient
Explore the patient's beliefs about diet, diabetes, and heart failure using open-ended, motivational interviewing techniques
Formulate a PES statement and propose 2-3 simple, concrete, patient-centered next steps

facts.says: I get full real fast, even if I only eat a little bit. It's annoying.

facts.says: Lunch is small, whatever's quick. Sandwich, maybe.

facts.says: Fruit's got a lot of sugar in it, right? I figured I should just stay away from it now.

facts.says: That pill upsets my stomach sometimes. And I don't really feel different whether I take it or not.

facts.says: Yeah, my pants are looser. Didn't really try to lose weight though.

facts.says: I think it's 'cause I just don't eat as much anymore. Food doesn't go down easy.

facts.says: But if I'm too skinny, don't I get weak? I don't want to end up frail either.

facts.says: I don't want to end up a burden on my son. That's the big thing for me.

facts.says: Work stresses me out, family stuff too sometimes. I don't really have a way to deal with it, I just push through.

mismatches.patientClaim: He states he takes metformin daily with dinner, 'mostly,' and frames it as a consistent habit even though he admits to occasionally forgetting.
mismatches.recordEvidence: Pharmacy refill history shows metformin was last filled 68 days ago with a pattern of recurring gaps over the past 6 months, while his heart failure medications show on-schedule refills every ~10-12 days as expected.
mismatches.teachingPoint: Self-reported adherence often overestimates actual medication-taking behavior. Refill/pharmacy records can reveal gaps that patients may not fully recognize or may minimize; this is a cue to explore barriers (GI side effects, perceived lack of benefit) non-judgmentally using motivational interviewing rather than confronting the discrepancy directly.

answerKey.primaryProblem: Poorly controlled Type 2 Diabetes with unintentional weight loss and inadequate oral intake related to early satiety, in the context of NYHA Class C heart failure
differential: Inadequate oral intake (NI-2.1) related to early satiety and irregular/skipped meals as evidenced by 6.5% unintentional weight loss over 6 months and BMI 19.0

Food- and nutrition-related knowledge deficit (NB-1.1) related to lack of understanding of the relationship between dietary pattern, heart failure, and glycemic control as evidenced by patient statements that heart and sugar problems are unrelated

Inconsistent carbohydrate intake / disordered meal pattern (NI-5.8.2 or NB-1.5) related to large, late evening meals and skipped breakfast as evidenced by diet history and post-meal palpitation reports
Altered nutrition-related laboratory values (NC-2.2) related to uncontrolled diabetes as evidenced by HbA1c 9.2% and random glucose 245 mg/dL
keyFindings: BMI 19.0 kg/m^2 with unintentional weight loss of 10 lbs (6.5%) over 6 months - nutritionally significant
HbA1c 9.2% and random glucose 245 mg/dL indicating poorly controlled diabetes despite inconsistent metformin use
Irregular meal pattern: skipped breakfast, small lunch, large late dinner (8-9 PM) associated with early satiety, fullness, and post-meal palpitations
Fruit and dairy avoidance based on misconceptions, narrowing nutrient variety (fiber, potassium, calcium, vitamin C)
Inconsistent fluid intake with risk of dehydration, notable given diuretic-adjacent heart failure regimen (though no fluid restriction currently ordered)
Mismatch between reported 'mostly consistent' metformin adherence and refill records showing significant gaps, linked to GI side effect fears and perceived lack of benefit
Belief that heart failure and diabetes are separate, independently managed conditions, reflecting a knowledge gap about the role of diet in both
Fear of weight gain worsening heart failure versus fear of being 'too skinny'/frail, creating ambivalence about increasing intake
Financial barriers to fresh produce and fatigue-limited meal preparation capacity
Normal multiple EGD findings ruling out structural GI cause for early satiety, supporting a functional/meal-pattern-related or cardiac-related etiology
plan: Formulate and document PES statement: 'Inadequate oral intake related to early satiety and irregular meal pattern as evidenced by 6.5% unintentional weight loss over 6 months and BMI 19.0 kg/m^2'

Recommend smaller, more frequent meals (5-6 small meals/day) distributing intake earlier in the day to reduce single-meal volume and post-dinner symptoms, while preserving total caloric/protein adequacy (~1850-2000 kcal, 70-80g protein/day)

Provide simple education connecting diet, blood glucose, and heart failure symptoms using plain language and the patient's preferred level of detail; correct misconception that fruit must be avoided entirely (recommend whole fruit in moderate, consistent portions as part of carbohydrate counting)

Address metformin adherence barriers collaboratively using motivational interviewing (explore GI side effect concerns and perceived lack of benefit) and recommend patient discuss timing/formulation (e.g., extended release) with prescribing provider rather than dietitian independently adjusting medication
Encourage small, consistent fluid intake throughout the day given no current fluid restriction, while coordinating with cardiology if restrictions are added later
Discuss appropriate reintroduction of lactose-containing foods in small amounts or lactose-free alternatives to support calcium/protein intake
Identify and connect patient with community resources (e.g., SNAP, local food assistance, diabetes self-management education program) to address financial barriers to fresh produce
Involve son in meal planning/grocery support in a way that respects patient's wish for independence, per patient's comfort level
Schedule follow-up nutrition visit to reassess weight trend, intake, and glycemic control, and coordinate with PCP/cardiology regarding medication adherence and symptom monitoring
redFlags: Unintentional weight loss >5% in 6 months with BMI near underweight threshold in setting of chronic heart failure - risk for cardiac cachexia if trend continues
Irregular heart rate (88 bpm, irregular) with post-meal palpitations - warrants communication to medical team, not solely a nutrition issue
HbA1c 9.2% indicating significantly uncontrolled diabetes with inconsistent medication adherence - risk for progression/complications
Elevated creatinine (1.3) with reduced eGFR (67) - relevant to future medication dosing and electrolyte monitoring, flag for medical team awareness
educationPoints: Diabetes and heart failure are interconnected: dietary patterns (meal timing, portion size, carbohydrate distribution) affect both blood sugar control and cardiac symptom burden, they are not separate systems to manage independently
Unintentional weight loss in heart failure is a warning sign, not necessarily a positive outcome, and differs from intentional weight loss for cardiovascular risk reduction
Smaller, more frequent meals distributed across the day can reduce early satiety-related symptoms and post-meal palpitations while supporting adequate nutrient intake
Whole fruit in consistent, moderate portions can fit into a diabetes meal plan and does not need to be eliminated; pairing with protein/fat can blunt glycemic response
Self-reported medication adherence can differ from actual adherence; open, non-judgmental conversation about barriers (side effects, perceived benefit) is more productive than confrontation
Simple, concrete, stepwise changes are more sustainable than complex overhauls, particularly given this patient's stated preferences and barriers (fatigue, low health literacy, cost)

profile.summary: A 59-year-old man with NYHA Class C heart failure and newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes presents for telehealth nutrition assessment with early satiety, fatigue, and unintentional weight loss, while holding the belief that his heart and diabetes conditions are unrelated and manageable through medication alone. The case teaches application of the Nutrition Care Process to a complex cardiometabolic patient, including recognition of a medication adherence mismatch (reported vs. refill-confirmed metformin use) and use of motivational interviewing to address low health literacy, financial barriers, and competing fears about weight gain versus frailty.
